passage:
'Sit still, Noor, or the oil will go in your eyes.' Nani's fingers pressed warm coconut oil into her scalp.
'Tell the one about the flood, Nani. When you were small.'
'Again? You've heard it fifty times.'
'Fifty-one, then.'
Nani laughed. 'The river came right up to our steps. My father put us children on the roof with the goat.'
'The goat's name was Badal,' Noor said.
'You remember everything.'
'Why didn't you go to the school building?'
'Good question. It was on lower ground. Your great-grandfather was wiser than he looked.'
Tanvir poked his head round the door. 'Is it the goat story? I want the goat story!'
'Sit, then. You're next.'
'I don't have long hair!'
'Then you get the oil only.' Noor giggled and leaned back against Nani's knees.

qa.q: What was the goat's name?
qa.a: Badal.

qa.q: How does Noor feel during the hair-oiling stories?
qa.a: Warm, loved and content; she asks for the story again and leans back against Nani's knees 🤍

qa.q: What does Noor do that makes the stories matter?
qa.a: She listens, remembers details like the goat's name, and asks questions such as why they didn't go to the school building.

qa.q: How does Nani feel when Noor remembers everything?
qa.a: Pleased and touched; she laughs and praises Noor's memory.

grounding: A girl loves her grandmother's stories while her hair is oiled, listening, asking questions and remembering.

passage: Every winter Sunday in Kolkata, Thakuma oiled my hair on the terrace, and my cousin Indu and I took turns sitting on the low stool in front of her. I'm Bidisha, and those mornings are the warmest thing I remember. The mustard oil smelled sharp, the sun was soft, and Thakuma told stories: how she walked to school with a lantern in Barisal, how she once hid a stray kitten in her rice tin. I always asked questions. 'What colour was the kitten? Did your mother find out?' Indu said I asked too many. Thakuma said questions keep stories alive. Now I write them in a green notebook, so I won't forget. Even today, whenever my hair is oiled, I can hear her voice.

qa.q: Where did Thakuma hide a stray kitten?
qa.a: In her rice tin.

qa.q: How does Bidisha feel remembering those Sunday mornings?
qa.a: Warm and loved; Bidisha calls them the warmest thing remembered and can still hear Thakuma's voice.

qa.q: What does Bidisha do to keep the stories?
qa.a: Asked questions while listening, and now writes the stories in a green notebook.

qa.q: How does Thakuma see Bidisha's questions?
qa.a: As a good thing; she says questions keep stories alive.

grounding: A child looks back on a grandmother's stories told while oiling hair, and keeps them by asking and writing them down.

passage: 'Zeenat, don't take the shortcut by the canal, the mud is slippery,' Dadajaan said from his charpai, for the third time that morning. Zeenat rolled her eyes so hard that Jahnavi, waiting at the gate, giggled. 'I know, Dadajaan! You say it every single day!' The words came out sharper than she meant. Dadajaan went quiet and looked down at his prayer beads. All the way to school, taking the long road round, Zeenat felt a pinch in her chest. The canal path was slippery, actually. And he said it because he had fallen there once, years ago. That afternoon she sat beside his charpai. 'Sorry for snapping. Tell me again about when you fell?' He smiled and told her, and she listened, even though she knew the story.

qa.q: Which shortcut did Dadajaan warn about?
qa.a: The shortcut by the canal.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling on the long road to school?
qa.a: Guilty and uneasy about snapping at Dadajaan, who had gone quiet.

qa.q: How did Zeenat repair things?
qa.a: She said sorry and asked to hear his story again, listening patiently even though she knew it.

qa.q: How might Dadajaan have felt when Zeenat snapped?
qa.a: Hurt and a little embarrassed; he went quiet and looked down at his prayer beads.

grounding: A village girl irritated by her grandfather's repeated advice snaps at him, then apologises and listens.

passage: Every morning in their Hanoi apartment, Ông said the same thing as Tuan tied his shoes: 'Wear the jacket. The wind gets into your chest.' Tuan was eleven and never felt cold. Today his friend Emil, visiting from Denmark, was waiting at the door, and Tuan felt his cheeks go warm. He almost said, 'Ông, you're so old-fashioned.' He could feel the words in his mouth. Instead he took a breath. 'Thank you, Ông. I'll keep it in my bag, and if I'm cold, I'll wear it.' Ông nodded, satisfied. On the stairs Emil said, 'My grandma tells me the same thing about hats.' Tuan laughed. At evening football, the wind picked up. He pulled on the jacket and said nothing, but he smiled.

qa.q: Where did Tuan say he'd keep the jacket?
qa.a: In his bag.

qa.q: What was Tuan feeling when Ông repeated the advice in front of Emil?
qa.a: Embarrassed and irritated, almost calling Ông old-fashioned.

qa.q: What did Tuan do instead of a rude reply?
qa.a: He thanked Ông and made his own choice: carry the jacket and wear it if he got cold.

qa.q: How did Ông feel about Tuan's answer?
qa.a: Satisfied and respected; he nodded.

grounding: A boy irritated by his grandfather's repeated advice listens politely and still makes his own choice.

passage: 'Tushar, you told your mother "Dadi lets me," didn't you? Come, let your Deepika Nani tell you something. My own grandmother spoiled me rotten. Jalebis before dinner, no sweeping, stories till midnight. My mother had rules: homework first, one sweet only. Once I stamped my foot and said, "Ammamma says I don't have to!" in front of both of them. My grandmother's face fell. My mother went red. That night Ammamma told me, "My love is a holiday, kanna. Your mother's rules are your home. Don't make us fight." After that, I enjoyed my jalebis at her place and did my sweeping at home. Both of them loved me. They just loved me in different ways.'

qa.q: What sweets did young Deepika get before dinner?
qa.a: Jalebis.

qa.q: What was young Deepika feeling when she stamped her foot?
qa.a: Frustrated and defiant, wanting to use Ammamma's softness against her mother's rules.

qa.q: What choice in the story fixed things?
qa.a: Enjoying the treats at Ammamma's place while following her mother's rules at home, without setting them against each other.

qa.q: How did Ammamma feel when Deepika used her against her mother?
qa.a: Hurt and uncomfortable; her face fell, and later she asked Deepika not to make them fight.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being spoiled by her own grandmother, and learning not to use that love against her mother's rules.

passage: Exams started tomorrow, the inverter had died in the power cut, and Gurleen was revising by candlelight at the dining table with her friend Zainab. Biji shuffled in with a steel plate piled with pinnis. 'Enough books, puttar. Eat, then sleep. I'll tell your mother you studied plenty.' Gurleen's mouth watered. Mummy's rule was clear: finish the chapter, then treats. It would be so easy to say later, 'Biji said I could.' Gurleen took one pinni and grinned. 'Thank you, Biji. One now, the rest after chapter six?' Biji laughed and pinched her cheek. 'Your mother trained you well.' Zainab took one too. When Mummy came home, Gurleen hugged her and said, 'Biji brought pinnis. We saved most for after.'

qa.q: What was on Biji's steel plate?
qa.a: Pinnis.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when Biji offered to cover for her?
qa.a: Tempted and happy, loving Biji's treat, but not wanting to set Biji against Mummy.

qa.q: How did Gurleen enjoy Biji's love without breaking Mummy's rule?
qa.a: She took one pinni, thanked Biji and saved the rest for after chapter six, then told Mummy honestly.

qa.q: How did Biji take Gurleen's answer?
qa.a: Fondly; she laughed, pinched her cheek and said her mother had trained her well.

grounding: During a power cut before exams a girl enjoys her grandmother's treats without using her against her mother's rules.

passage:
Saturday. Kashish kept one chair empty at her birthday table, right next to hers. Shreya had promised, pinky-promised, that she would come. The cake was cut, the games were played, and the chair stayed empty. Kashish smiled for the photos and cried in the bathroom afterwards.
Sunday. She typed an angry message: 'Don't bother talking to me again.' She stared at it, then deleted it.
Monday. At the school gate, Kashish took a breath. 'Shreya, you promised to come on Saturday. I kept a chair for you. It really hurt.' Shreya's face crumpled. 'My Nani fell, and we rushed to the hospital. I didn't have your number with me. I'm so sorry.' Kashish felt the hurt loosen a little. 'Is she okay?' 'She's okay now.'

qa.q: What did Kashish keep empty?
qa.a: One chair at her birthday table, right next to hers.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel when the chair stayed empty?
qa.a: Hurt and let down; she smiled for the photos but cried in the bathroom.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than the angry message?
qa.a: Telling Shreya calmly how it felt and giving her the chance to explain.

qa.q: What was it like for Shreya when Kashish spoke to her?
qa.a: Painful and guilty; her face crumpled because she had a real reason but had still broken her promise.

grounding: Over three days a girl hurt by a friend missing her birthday chooses to tell her calmly and ask why, instead of snapping.

passage: 'Vinita, your friend didn't come to your party and now you won't speak to her? Let your Urmila Aaji tell you what I did once. I was nine. My friend Shobha promised to come for my birthday puja and never came. At school I turned my back on her. When she tried to explain, I said, "Liar," and walked off. I didn't talk to her for a whole month. It felt strong, but inside I was still hurting, every single day. Then my mother asked, "Did you ever tell her how it felt?" I hadn't. So I did. Shobha cried and told me her father had lost his job that week and she had no gift to bring. She had been too ashamed to come. A whole month, wasted.'

qa.q: What did young Urmila call Shobha?
qa.a: Liar.

qa.q: What was young Urmila feeling during the month of silence?
qa.a: Still hurt every day, even though turning her back felt strong.

qa.q: What choice in the story finally helped?
qa.a: Telling Shobha how it felt and hearing her reason, instead of refusing to talk.

qa.q: How had Shobha felt about missing the puja?
qa.a: Ashamed, because her father had lost his job that week and she had no gift to bring.

grounding: A grandmother recalls refusing to speak to a friend who broke a promise, and how telling her calmly revealed the reason.

passage: 'Rukmini, you're not sure whether to forgive Pallavi? Sit here with your Vandana Maasi. When I was ten, my friend Leela told the whole class I was scared of the dark and slept with a lamp on. I wanted to vanish. Two days later she came to my house with her mother's pedas and cried. "They were teasing me and I blurted it out. I'm sorry." I could see she meant it. So I forgave her. I let the anger go, but I didn't tell her any secrets for a long while. When she slipped up again with a small thing the next year, I said straight away, "Leela, that's twice. I need you to stop." She did. We're still friends. Forgiving isn't pretending it didn't hurt, beta.'

qa.q: What did Leela bring when she came to apologise?
qa.a: Her mother's pedas.

qa.q: How did young Vandana feel after Leela told the class her secret?
qa.a: Humiliated and betrayed; she wanted to vanish.

qa.q: What choice did Vandana make when Leela slipped up again?
qa.a: She said straight away that it was the second time and asked Leela to stop.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt coming to apologise?
qa.a: Ashamed and sorry; she cried and explained she had blurted it out under teasing.

grounding: An aunt recalls forgiving a friend who apologised, staying careful for a while, and speaking up when it happened again.

passage: The science fair started in an hour, and Alka had promised to bring the batteries for their windmill model. She arrived empty-handed and red-eyed. 'I'm so sorry, Nirmala. My little brother had fever all night and I forgot everything.' Nirmala's first feeling was a hot flash of anger. Their model would just sit there. But Alka's hands were shaking. Nirmala took a breath. 'Okay. I'm annoyed, but I believe you. Let's fix it.' They ran to the stationery shop by the gate, counted their coins, and bought two batteries just in time. The blades spun. Later, Nirmala thought it over. She had forgiven Alka. But for the next project, she'd carry the important things herself. And if Alka forgot again, she would say so.

qa.q: What had Alka promised to bring?
qa.a: The batteries for their windmill model.

qa.q: What was Nirmala's first feeling when Alka arrived empty-handed?
qa.a: A hot flash of anger that their model would just sit there.

qa.q: How did Nirmala forgive without pretending nothing happened?
qa.a: She said she was annoyed but believed Alka, fixed the problem with her, and decided to carry important things herself next time.

qa.q: What was it like for Alka arriving without the batteries?
qa.a: Stressful and guilty after a night of her brother's fever; her hands were shaking.

grounding: An hour before a science fair a girl forgives her friend's broken promise, stays careful, and plans to speak up if it recurs.

passage:
'Hrithik! Why are you hiding behind the notice board?'
Hrithik winced. 'I'm not hiding.'
'You've avoided me for three days.' Hansa folded her arms. 'You promised to help me practise my elocution speech on Sunday. I waited at the park for an hour.'
His face burned. He had gone to his cousin's cricket match instead and forgotten. Every time he saw her, the shame got worse.
'I... I forgot. I went to a match. I'm really sorry, Hansa. I was too embarrassed to say it.'
She was quiet. 'You could have just told me.'
'I know. Can I make it up? The contest's next Friday. I'll listen to your speech every day at lunch this week.'
Hansa sighed. 'Every day?'
'Every single day.'
'Fine. Starting now.'

qa.q: How long did Hansa wait at the park?
qa.a: An hour.

qa.q: Why had Hrithik been hiding from Hansa?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and embarrassed about breaking his promise, and the shame grew each time he saw her.

qa.q: How did Hrithik start to repair things?
qa.a: He told the truth, apologised, and offered to hear her speech every day at lunch.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel about being avoided?
qa.a: Hurt and annoyed; she would rather he had simply told her.

grounding: A boy too embarrassed to face the friend whose promise he broke finally tells the truth, apologises and makes up for it.

passage: Last term I promised Shalini I'd be her partner for the dance competition. Then the most popular girl in class asked me, and I said yes without thinking. I'm Jasleen, and I spent a week hiding from Shalini, going to the library at lunch and taking the other staircase. My stomach felt heavy every time I saw her plait at the end of the corridor. Hiding just made it bigger. Finally I wrote her a note: 'I broke my promise because I wanted to look cool. That was wrong. I'm sorry.' I slipped it into her bag and waited, feeling sick. The next day she found me. 'It hurt,' she said. 'But thanks for being honest.' After that I helped her practise with her new partner every afternoon.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen go at lunch to hide?
qa.a: The library.

qa.q: What did Jasleen's heavy stomach show?
qa.a: Jasleen felt ashamed and guilty about breaking the promise to Shalini.

qa.q: What finally started to heal things?
qa.a: Writing Shalini an honest note that admitted the real reason and said sorry, then helping her practise.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel about the broken promise and the note?
qa.a: Hurt by the broken promise, but thankful that Jasleen was honest.

grounding: A child hides from a friend after breaking a promise, then admits the truth in a note and makes amends.

passage: Valentina had promised to go to the Oslo science museum with Lars on Saturday. She had also promised to return his bike lock, to come to his football match, and to save him a seat at the school concert. She hadn't done any of it. On Saturday morning, when her message came, 'sorry cant make it!! next week promise', Lars didn't feel angry any more. He just felt tired. He replied, 'No worries.' Then he called his neighbour Ole and went to the museum with him instead. On Monday Valentina asked him to help with her poster for Friday's project. Lars helped her at lunch; he liked her jokes. But when she said, 'And you'll bring the glue on Friday?' he said, 'You bring the glue. I'll bring the paper.'

qa.q: Who did Lars go to the museum with?
qa.a: His neighbour Ole.

qa.q: How did Lars feel when Valentina's message came?
qa.a: Tired rather than angry, worn down by being let down again and again.

qa.q: How does Lars protect himself without being cruel?
qa.a: He stays friendly and helps with her poster, but no longer counts on her for important things like the glue.

qa.q: How might Valentina see Lars's 'You bring the glue'?
qa.a: She might be surprised, noticing that he no longer relies on her promises.

grounding: After repeated broken promises a boy stops counting on his friend for important things while staying friendly.

passage: In the girls' hostel, Madhuri had the only alarm clock in Room 12, and three times she had promised to wake Ayesha for early swimming practice. Three times she had slept through it, and Ayesha had been scolded by the coach for coming late. The fourth night, Madhuri said, 'Tomorrow for sure. Trust me.' Ayesha felt a small, sad hardness in her chest. She smiled and said, 'Thanks, but I'll manage.' Then she asked the warden to lend her a wind-up clock and set it herself. It rang in the dark. Madhuri was snoring. Ayesha tucked Madhuri's blanket back over her foot and went to practice on time. At lunch they still shared pickle and giggled over comics. Ayesha just didn't trust Madhuri with her mornings any more.

qa.q: Which room were they in?
qa.a: Room 12.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when Madhuri said 'Trust me'?
qa.a: Sad and wary; after being let down three times, she no longer believed the promise.

qa.q: How did Ayesha protect herself while staying kind?
qa.a: She borrowed a clock and woke herself, but still shared lunch and jokes with Madhuri.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel if she noticed Ayesha's new clock?
qa.a: Perhaps a bit embarrassed, realising her broken promises had cost Ayesha's trust.

grounding: In a hostel a girl let down repeatedly stops relying on her friend's promises but stays friendly.

subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
passage: In the school library, Ramesh Sir held up a book with its cover ripped off. 'Lalremsiami, this was issued to you. Explain.' Heat flooded her face. The class turned to stare. She wanted to shout, It wasn't me! Instead she gripped the desk and took a breath. 'Sir, I returned it on Monday. It was fine then. You stamped it, and the register should show the date. After me, it went to someone else.' Ramesh Sir frowned and opened the register. His finger stopped on a line. 'Hmm. It was issued again on Tuesday.' He put the book down. 'I was wrong to blame you. I'm sorry.' At home, Lalremsiami told her mother, still shaky. Her mother said, 'You did it right. If it happens again, I'll come in with you.'

qa.q: On which day did Lalremsiami return the book?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when Ramesh Sir blamed her?
qa.a: Angry and embarrassed, hot with the unfairness of it; she wanted to shout but gripped the desk instead.

qa.q: What made her explanation work?
qa.a: She stayed calm, gave facts about the return and the stamp, and asked for a fair check of the register.

qa.q: How did Ramesh Sir react once he checked?
qa.a: He saw his mistake and apologised to her.

grounding: A girl wrongly blamed by a teacher explains calmly with facts, is cleared, and her mother offers support.

subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
passage:
Monday. The class plant pot lay smashed on the floor, and Mrs D'Souza walked in to find Harsha pointing at Madhuri. 'She was nearest!' Mrs D'Souza sent Madhuri to stand outside. Madhuri's chest burned with unfairness. She had been at the window watching the rain. She cried in the corridor and said nothing. That evening Papa listened to the whole story. 'Let's write down what happened, calmly. Just the facts.' Madhuri wrote it: where she was, who was near the pot, who saw.
Tuesday. Papa came with her before class. Madhuri read her note to Mrs D'Souza, voice wobbling but steady. Mrs D'Souza asked two other children. Then she said, 'I rushed. I'm sorry, Madhuri.' Harsha looked at the floor.

qa.q: Where had Madhuri been when the pot broke?
qa.a: At the window watching the rain.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling in the corridor?
qa.a: Burning with unfairness and hurt, so upset she cried and said nothing.

qa.q: How did Papa help Madhuri get a fair look?
qa.a: He listened, helped her write the facts calmly, and came with her to school so she could read them to the teacher.

qa.q: What might Harsha have felt when the teacher apologised?
qa.a: Guilty and embarrassed, since Harsha looked at the floor.

grounding: Over two days a girl wrongly blamed by a teacher writes down the facts with her father's help and is heard fairly.

subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
passage: In Class 6, Kalyani and I were caught near the broken science-lab window. I'm Farhan. It was Kalyani's ball that broke it, but when Sir asked, she said nothing. She just looked at me. I got a note home and had to miss football for a week. I lay awake feeling as if something inside had cracked. For three days I didn't speak to her. Then I made myself say it. 'Kalyani, I saw you stay quiet. You let me take it.' Her eyes filled. 'I was scared I'd be dropped from the sports team. I'm sorry.' I listened. I understood a bit. But I didn't say 'It's fine,' because it wasn't. I told her I needed time. It took most of the term before I trusted her again.

qa.q: How long did Farhan have to miss football?
qa.a: A week.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel lying awake?
qa.a: Betrayed and hurt, as if something inside had cracked.

qa.q: How did Farhan handle it?
qa.a: Told Kalyani plainly what had been seen, listened to her reason, and took time before trusting her again.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani stay quiet, according to her?
qa.a: She was scared of being dropped from the sports team, and she felt sorry afterwards.

grounding: A child whose friend let them take the blame tells her so, hears her out, and rebuilds trust slowly.

subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
passage:
Class teacher's note, by Manjula Rao, Friday.
This morning I found chalk drawings all over the new board and, after a quick look, sent Ganga to the office because she was standing nearest. At lunch Ganga came back to me, very quietly. She said her friend Meghna had made the drawings and let Ganga take the blame. Ganga's hands were clenched and her voice shook: 'She saw them take me and didn't say anything.' I asked Meghna, who admitted it and cried. I apologised to Ganga for not checking. Ganga told Meghna, 'I saw what you did,' and listened to her reason. She did not hug her. She told me she would decide about the friendship 'later, maybe'. I think that is wise.

qa.q: Where was Ganga sent?
qa.a: To the office.

qa.q: What did Ganga's clenched hands and shaking voice show?
qa.a: She felt deeply betrayed and angry that Meghna watched her take the blame.

qa.q: How did Ganga handle Meghna afterwards?
qa.a: She told Meghna she saw what she did, listened to her reason, and chose to decide about the friendship slowly.

qa.q: How might Meghna feel after admitting it?
qa.a: Ashamed and sorry; she cried when asked.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a girl betrayed by a friend who let her take the blame, facing the friend and deciding slowly about trust.

subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
passage: The school bus for the zoo trip was leaving in twenty minutes, and Ankita was sitting outside the principal's office, not allowed to go. Someone had spilled paint on the new bulletin board, and Ankita had been standing next to it. It was Elizabeth who had knocked the jar. She had said nothing, and now her stomach felt sick. Every minute, the bus engine rumbled louder in the yard. She could get on and forget it. Instead, legs trembling, she knocked on the office door. 'Ma'am, it was me. I knocked the paint over. Ankita didn't do anything.' The principal looked at her for a long moment. 'Thank you for telling me.' Ankita was allowed on the bus. Elizabeth sat beside her. 'I'm really sorry I let you take it.'

qa.q: Where was the school trip going?
qa.a: To the zoo.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth's stomach feel sick?
qa.a: She felt guilty and afraid, knowing Ankita was being punished for what Elizabeth had done.

qa.q: What brave steps did Elizabeth take?
qa.a: She admitted it to the principal before the bus left, then apologised to Ankita.

qa.q: What was it like for Ankita outside the office?
qa.a: Unfair and upsetting; she was being kept from the trip for something she didn't do.

grounding: With a bus about to leave, a girl who let her friend take the blame out of fear admits the truth and apologises.

subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
passage: It was Ira's elbow that knocked the water bottle over the class's clay model of the Red Fort, turning one wall to mud. Mrs Arora walked in, saw Sudha holding the empty bottle to pick it up, and said, 'Sudha! After all our work!' Sudha opened her mouth, looked at Ira, and closed it. Ira said nothing. At home in their Karol Bagh flat, Ira couldn't eat her rajma. Her stomach churned all night. The fear of being scolded had gone quiet; now there was only the picture of Sudha's face. Next morning she went straight to the staffroom. 'Ma'am, it was me. Sudha only picked up the bottle.' Mrs Arora sighed, but nodded. Then Ira found Sudha by the water cooler. 'I'm sorry. I was scared. That's not an excuse.'

qa.q: What did Ira's elbow knock over?
qa.a: The water bottle.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling that night in the Karol Bagh flat?
qa.a: Sick with guilt; the fear had faded, but regret about Sudha's face stayed.

qa.q: What did Ira do the next morning?
qa.a: She told Mrs Arora the truth and then apologised to Sudha without making excuses.

qa.q: Why might Sudha have stayed silent when blamed?
qa.a: She may have hoped Ira would speak up, or not wanted to get her friend into trouble.

grounding: A girl who let her friend take the blame out of fear feels regret overnight, then admits it to the teacher and apologises.
